title: Jeremiah 51:59–64
context: Jeremiah narrates how he gave Seraiah son of Neriah, the chief quartermaster, a book of these words against Babylon when Seraiah went with Zedekiah to Babylon in the king’s fourth year (51:59–60). Seraiah is to read it there, bind a stone to it, and cast it into the Euphrates, saying that Babylon will sink and not rise (51:61–64). Seraiah’s family line matches Baruch’s in 32:12. The trip is otherwise unrecorded in detail, and dates proposed for it are held with caution. The closing words, “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah,” lead into chapter 52.

verses.text: The word which Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah the king of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. Now Seraiah was chief quartermaster.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah narrates the word he gave to “Seraiah the son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah,” who went to Babylon with Zedekiah. Arminian readers note that Baruch has the same lineage in 32:12, so Seraiah may be his brother.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the shared family line with Baruch in 32:12. The visit in Zedekiah’s fourth year is not described elsewhere in detail, and readers in this tradition hold its circumstances with caution.

verses.text: Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come on Babylon, even all these words that are written concerning Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: “Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come on Babylon.” Arminian readers see the prophet committing the oracle to writing, giving it lasting witness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the written word as a testimony. Readers in this tradition note that writing plays an important role in Jeremiah, as in chapter 36, cited by reference.

verses.text: Jeremiah said to Seraiah, “When you come to Babylon, then see that you read all these words,
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah said to Seraiah, “When you come to Babylon, then see that you read all these words.” Arminian readers see the word proclaimed even in the enemy’s capital.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s word announced in Babylon itself. Readers in this tradition note the boldness of reading judgment on the empire in its own city.

verses.text: and say, ‘LORD, you have spoken concerning this place, to cut it off, that no one will dwell in it, neither man nor animal, but that it will be desolate forever.’
verses.arminianNotes: “LORD, you have spoken concerning this place, to cut it off.” Arminian readers see Seraiah instructed to address God, confirming that the word of judgment comes from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prayer acknowledging that the LORD has spoken. Readers in this tradition see the reading as an act of faith in God’s word before its fulfillment.

verses.text: It will be, when you have finished reading this book, that you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the middle of the Euphrates.
verses.arminianNotes: “… you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the middle of the Euphrates.” Arminian readers see a symbolic act that enacts the message of Babylon’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a prophetic sign-act. Revelation 18:21 pictures a millstone cast into the sea as a sign of Babylon’s fall, cited here by reference; readers in this tradition hold it as a later reuse.

verses.text: Then you shall say, ‘Thus will Babylon sink, and will not rise again because of the evil that I will bring on her; and they will be weary.’ ” Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
verses.arminianNotes: “Thus will Babylon sink, and will not rise again.” Then the narrator adds, “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.” Arminian readers see the sign completed and the book’s collection of his words closed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the sinking scroll as a picture of Babylon’s end. The closing note marks the end of Jeremiah’s words before chapter 52, and readers in this tradition note the editorial transition.
